title: GPU runtime profiling: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graphs - deep dive (with Luminis Systems)
topics: VPC / on-prem constraints and network egress
summary: Deep technical session to profile Redwood GPU runtime with Luminis's internal model. Covered kernel selection heuristics, observed throughput/latency tradeoffs between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, CUDA graph warmup effects, KV cache hit patterns, and quantization impacts. Agreed next steps: run end-to-end benchmark on Luminis staging, share profiling artifacts (cupti/cuda-memtrace/flamegraphs), and evaluate a pilot dedicated cluster with VPC peering and KMS integration.
action_items: Jordan Lee: share benchmark spreadsheet + raw nvprof/cupti logs by 2026-12-24
Priya Menon: produce kernel-selection summary + suggested kernel override knobs by 2026-12-26
Marta Ruiz: provide representative eval prompts + 10k request trace anonymized by 2026-12-23
Samir Patel: open ticket with infra to test VPC peering and egress baseline by 2026-12-28
next_steps: Redwood to run TensorRT-LLM and vLLM side-by-side on Luminis staging (same model/seq length) and provide token-level latency distribution
Customer to share model config + sample traffic profile
Schedule follow-up demo to review benchmark results week of 2026-12-29
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-22
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Menon (Redwood SE - Inference), Kelly Tran (Redwood), Alex Moretti (CTO - Luminis), Marta Ruiz (Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra), Ivy Chen (Security)

00:00 Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Jordan from Redwood, really excited for a deep dive. we've got priya on the call to go through the profiling details, priya do you want to kick off?
00:12 Priya Menon: yeah thanks jordan hello all, hi alex, marta, samir — quick agenda, we'll run through our profiling approach, show kernel selection logs, then side-by-side TensorRT-LLM and vLLM runs, and finish with cuda graphs + warmup behavior. sound good?
00:30 Alex Moretti: sounds great, we're mainly focused on latency p95 and token throughput at seq lengths 512 and 2048, also curious about kv cache warmup for chat-style workloads.
00:42 Marta Ruiz: yep and quantization is a big one — last time we saw int8 artifacts for code-gen prompts, so we want to understand tradeoffs.
00:52 Priya Menon: noted — we'll show per-op breakdown and where quant introduces quality regressions vs speedups.
01:05 Jordan Lee: also, samir raised network/VPC constraints — so we'll mention on-prem/VPC peering costs and how caching plays with private deployments.

05:10 Priya Menon: okay jumping into profiling methodology — we use a mixture of nvprof / Nsight metrics, cupti traces for kernel timings, and our runtime's internal kernel-selection trace (that's the decision log where we pick cuBLAS vs CUTLASS vs TensorRT kernels). we capture the first 30 tokens cold-start then prefix warmup and steady-state.
05:40 Priya Menon: one confusing bit we often see: vLLM tends to give lower end-to-end latency for smaller batch sizes due to lighter kernel launch overhead, but TensorRT-LLM outperforms at higher throughput because of fused kernels and attention optimizations — caveat: depends on sequence length and kv cache hit rates.
06:05 Marta Ruiz: can you quantify "lower" and "outperforms"? like p50/p95 numbers?
06:12 Priya Menon: sure — on an A100 80GB, with a 13B decoder-only model at seq512, vLLM baseline p95 ~ 180ms per token at batch=1, TensorRT-LLM p95 ~ 220ms cold but after cuda-graph warmup and continuous batching p95 drops to ~120ms at throughput-optimized settings. those are rough but we will provide exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
06:45 Alex Moretti: interesting, so trt slower at first but better at throughput — that aligns with our observations. how long is warmup to get under 200ms?
06:52 Priya Menon: warmup varies — typical cuda-graph warmup is 3-10 iterations depending on kernel set and sequence length, sometimes more if model uses many attention heads and kv cache causes different kernel shapes. we show traces where the first 5 tokens have extra kernel launches.
07:10 Samir Patel: from infra side, does that warmup cost show up as GPU memory spikes or PCIe traffic? we need to know for capacity planning.
07:18 Priya Menon: mostly extra kernel launches and a little extra temporary memory; PCIe increases if we spill to host (rare on 80GB). memory stabilizes after steady-state. we attach memory timelines in the report.

12:02 Priya Menon: kernel selection — our runtime runs a heuristics pass: it evaluates operator shape (seq_len, kv_len, head_count, dim_k), then consults a kernel cost table (calibrated per-hardware) to pick between cuBLAS/FlashAttention/CUTLASS/TensorRT fused attention. we also fallback to vLLM-style kernels if TensorRT plugin isn't compatible.
12:32 Priya Menon: one customer question: sometimes we force a specific kernel when a plugin has numerical issues — we expose an override flag to pin kernels per-model if you need determinism.
12:48 Marta Ruiz: that's useful. what about mixed precision? we saw bit flips at 4-bit quantization on some arithmetic heavy prompts.
12:56 Priya Menon: yeah quantization is tricky — int8 usually safe with calibration but 4-bit (GPTQ/LLM.int4) can introduce hallucination in code-like prompts. best practice: run eval set with our quality monitoring. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles by workload.

18:20 Priya Menon: here's the side-by-side: we ran your 13B model with identical weights (converted to TRT-LLM engine) and also on vLLM with Triton kernels. Key observations: TRT-LLM gives 1.8-2.4x throughput improvement for seq>=1024 with batch>4; vLLM wins at batch=1 or conversational single-turn low-latency cases. p99 tails are better on TRT when continuous batching and caching are used.
18:51 Alex Moretti: what about reproducibility? we need to reproduce these numbers in our staging with same docker image.
18:57 Priya Menon: we'll share the dockerfile, the TRT conversion script, and exact cmdline plus the hardware profiles. note: TensorRT versions and driver compatibility affect kernel choice; we recommend matching driver/CUDA/CUDNN/TensorRT versions in staging.
19:12 Marta Ruiz: any gotchas with Triton server or does Redwood runtime abstract that?
19:18 Jordan Lee: Redwood runtime handles orchestration; for Private/VPC installs we ship a runtime that includes the exact TensorRT plugin versions. still you should pin the host driver to the tested matrix.

25:30 Priya Menon: CUDA Graphs — we instrumented graph capture and replay. benefit: removes launch overhead and gives stable p50, p95. downside: graphs are shape / size sensitive; if with kv cache the graph shape evolves, then you need multiple captured graphs or dynamic capture. capture strategy: capture at representative sequence lengths (e.g., 32, 512, 2048) and branch accordingly.
25:58 Samir Patel: does graph capture require restarting the process? how does that interact with rolling updates?
26:05 Priya Menon: capture is done at runtime; you can capture live when traffic patterns are steady. rolling updates: we recommend capture during canary after deploy. we also support pre-captured graph bundles to be loaded at startup.

30:40 Priya Menon: KV cache warmup — for chat flows where prefixes are long, the first generation will be expensive because we need to populate cache; subsequent tokens are cheap. we saw cache-hit ratio reach 95% after 1-2 turns for typical chat. but if users have many short-lived contexts, caching helps less.
31:05 Marta Ruiz: we have a mixed workload — long prefixes for context + many short queries. any guidance?
31:13 Priya Menon: use a hybrid policy: keep prefix caching for long-lived sessions and fall back to stateless for ephemeral requests. Redwood Optimize can suggest TTLs and per-route cache policies.

36:00 Priya Menon: quantization benchmarks — we ran fp16, int8 calibrated, and GPTQ 4-bit. fp16 is safe and gives ~1.6x over fp32. int8 ~2.2x but with some edge-case numerical deltas; 4-bit can be 3-4x but needs careful calibration and evaluation. for the customer's code-gen tests, we saw a small but measurable degradation in token-level accuracy for 4-bit.
36:36 Marta Ruiz: that's the risk we feared. is there an automated rollback if quality drops?
36:45 Jordan Lee: yes, Redwood's rollout policy supports canary with quality gates tied into eval sets; if regression exceeds threshold we auto-fallback to previous quant profile or a non-quantized build.

40:50 Ivy Chen: quick security question: if we do Private with VPC peering, how do we handle KMS and keys for model weights and logs?
40:58 Jordan Lee: we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and integrate with CEK. logs can be forwarded to your SIEM over TLS; audit logs can be retained in your account. for on-prem we can integrate with your HSM, and for hosted we support KMS key injection. we'll share the security docs.

45:20 Priya Menon: now some raw traces — (screen share) here's a cupti timeline showing kernel types color-coded. you can see the attention kernel using fused attention (TensorRT plugin) takes longer on first few invocations but amortizes when batched. the vLLM trace shows many smaller kernels with more frequent kernel launches.
45:45 Marta Ruiz: do you have flamegraphs for the whole token generation?
45:50 Priya Menon: yes, attached in the artifact bundle — we include per-thread GPU flamegraphs and CPU-GPU communication traces.

52:10 Alex Moretti: on numbers — can you commit to a bench that mimics our real traffic? our traffic is 70% chat (avg seq 800) and 30% short queries (seq 64) with 150 qps.
52:24 Priya Menon: we can run a mixed workload test. action: please send the anonymized 10k request trace — we'll run it and provide p50/p95/p99 and cost per token estimates on TRT-LLM vs vLLM and the Dedicated plan.

58:00 Samir Patel: about Dedicated clusters — what are network egress implications for VPC peering? are there extra costs for cross-AZ?
58:10 Jordan Lee: cross-AZ egress is cloud-billed; for Dedicated we recommend colocated nodes in same AZ or using a private interconnect; we'll include cost modeling in the sheet.

63:30 Priya Menon: open question we ran into — some third-party kernels choose slightly different reduction strategies which can shift numerical rounding and cause deviance on certain LLM attention patterns; we annotate these cases in our kernel selection trace and can force a deterministic kernel if needed.
63:55 Marta Ruiz: that's a big deal for us — determinism matters for model audits.
64:05 Priya Menon: understood — we can provision a deterministic runtime path that avoids non-deterministic kernels but it may cost on latency. we'll quantify tradeoffs.

70:00 Jordan Lee: recap — Redwood to run mixed-workload bench on Luminis staging, share raw traces + spreadsheet; Priya will summarize kernel selection decisions and knobs; Marta to share eval prompts and trace; Samir to validate VPC peering. we'll aim to reconvene next week.
70:28 Alex Moretti: thanks everyone, very helpful session. looking forward to the artifact pack.
70:36 Jordan Lee: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invite for the results review. bye.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]
